worked_solution:
To apply the ratio test we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{{4}^{n}{x}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{4}^{n+1}{x}^{n+1}}{(n+1)^{2}+4(n+1)}\cdot \frac{{n}^{2}+4n}{{4}^{n}{x}^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{4x({n}^{2}+4n)}{{n}^{2}+6n+5}| \\  & =|4x|\cdot {lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{2}+4n}{{n}^{2}+6n+5} \\  & =|4x|\cdot 1 \\  & =|4x|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for $|4x|<1,$ which means $|x|<\frac{1}{4}.$ So, the radius of convergence is $\frac{1}{4},$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{4}).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x|=\frac{1}{4},$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ and $x=\frac{1}{4}$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=\frac{1}{4}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{4}^{n}{x}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{4}^{n}{(1/4)}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+4n} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 5}+\frac{1}{2\cdot 6}+\frac{1}{3\cdot 7}+\frac{1}{4\cdot 8}+⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the direct comparison test with the convergent $p$-series $\sum \frac{1}{{n}^{2}}.$ So the endpoint $x=\frac{1}{4}$ is included in our interval.

- When $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{4}^{n}{x}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{4}^{n}{(-1/4)}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}+4n} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1\cdot 5}+\frac{1}{2\cdot 6}-\frac{1}{3\cdot 7}+\frac{1}{4\cdot 8}-⋯,\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test. So the endpoint $x=-\frac{1}{4}$ is included in our interval.

Therefore, the interval of convergence is $[-\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{4}],$ or equivalently, $-\frac{1}{4}\le x\le \frac{1}{4}.$

To apply the ratio test we define an=4nxnn2+4n. Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as n→∞:

L=limn→∞|an+1an|=limn→∞|4n+1xn+1(n+1)2+4(n+1)⋅n2+4n4nxn|=limn→∞|4x(n2+4n)n2+6n+5|=|4x|⋅limn→∞n2+4nn2+6n+5=|4x|⋅1=|4x|

The series converges if L<1. In this case, the convergence condition is satisfied for |4x|<1, which means |x|<14. So, the radius of convergence is 14, and the series converges for any x that lies in the open interval (−14,14).

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when L=1. So, when |x|=14, we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints x=−14 and x=14 need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

  • When x=14 we have ∑n=1∞4nxnn2+4n=∑n=1∞4n(1/4)nn2+4n=∑n=1∞1n2+4n=11⋅5+12⋅6+13⋅7+14⋅8+⋯, which is convergent by the direct comparison test with the convergent p-series ∑1n2. So the endpoint x=14 is included in our interval.

  • When x=−14 we have ∑n=1∞4nxnn2+4n=∑n=1∞4n(−1/4)nn2+4n=∑n=1∞(−1)nn2+4n=−11⋅5+12⋅6−13⋅7+14⋅8−⋯, which is convergent by the alternating series test. So the endpoint x=−14 is included in our interval.

Therefore, the interval of convergence is [−14,14], or equivalently, −14≤x≤14.
